summary: Defines the EAP early authentication problem, where a mobile device uses EAP to set up keying material on a target attachment point before it arrives. The document discusses the problem in detail. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It is like showing your ticket at the next building before you walk there, so you get in fast when you arrive.

questions: what is the eap early auth problem
subtitle: Pre-authenticating to a network before arriving to reduce handover delay.

tldr.problem: When mobile devices move between networks, the handover process includes authentication with the new network, introducing latency that affects real-time applications like VoIP.
tldr.mechanism: EAP early authentication lets a mobile device authenticate to a target network while still connected to the current one, establishing keying material in advance.
tldr.outcome: The authentication delay is incurred before the handover occurs rather than during it, reducing service disruption. Applicable to both intra-realm and inter-realm handovers.

today: RFC 5836 is an Informational RFC that identifies the early authentication problem and proposes solution models, but does not specify a protocol. The RFC highlights numerous unresolved issues in AAA protocols and architecture that would need to be addressed by future standards-track specifications. The problem remains relevant for mobile devices moving between networks and between access technologies.

sections.title: The Handover Authentication Problem
sections.content:
Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) early authentication addresses a specific problem: when a mobile device moves from one network attachment point to another, it must re-authenticate with the new network. This authentication process adds latency to the handover.

Real-time applications like Voice over IP have strict delay requirements. ITU-T Recommendation G.114 suggests that 150 milliseconds of end-to-end delay is acceptable, while 400 milliseconds or more becomes unacceptable. Streaming applications tolerate delays under 300 milliseconds. During a normal handover with full EAP authentication, the combined effect of layer 2 rebinding, layer 3 configuration, and authentication round trips often exceeds these limits, degrading voice quality or dropping connections.
sections.eli5: When you switch WiFi networks, the handover (connecting to the new one) takes time. If that time is too long, your call gets choppy or drops. Early authentication speeds this up by doing the checking beforehand.

sections.title: Why Handover Latency Matters
sections.content:
The handover process has two phases: preparation (discovering candidate networks) and execution (setting up layer 2 and layer 3 connectivity with the target attachment point). Handover execution includes network access authentication and authorization, which require interaction with a central authority, often an AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting) server.

In many cases, the AAA server may be distant from the mobile device, adding network latency to the authentication procedure. The delay is particularly acute when the mobile device must authenticate through its home realm when visiting a different network. This situation is common in mobile scenarios where a device roams between different service providers or between different access technologies such as WiFi and cellular networks.
sections.eli5: Authentication needs to check with a distant server that knows who you are. If that server is far away, the messages travel slowly. Early authentication does this check ahead of time, when you're not in a hurry to connect.

sections.title: Three Models of Early Authentication
sections.content:
The RFC describes three approaches to EAP early authentication. In the direct pre-authentication model, the mobile device discovers candidate authenticators and performs EAP authentication directly with each one over IP, without involving the current serving attachment point. The EAP traffic passes through the serving network as regular data traffic.

The indirect pre-authentication model assumes a trust relationship exists between the serving and candidate networks. The serving attachment point forwards EAP pre-authentication messages between the mobile device and candidate authenticators. This approach is necessary when the mobile device cannot discover candidate authenticators or cannot establish direct IP communication due to security or topology constraints.

The authenticated anticipatory keying model applies when no trust relationship exists between serving and candidate networks. The serving attachment point communicates directly with the AAA server to obtain keying material for the candidate attachment point, which receives and stores the material in advance.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to do early authentication: talk directly to the new network, have your current network relay the conversation, or have your current network get the keys from the authority and give them to the new network.

sections.title: Architectural Considerations
sections.content:
Two major architectural issues arise in early authentication: authenticator discovery and context binding. The mobile device (or serving attachment point) must discover the identity and address of candidate attachment points before authentication can occur. Methods such as IEEE 802.21 Information Service provide mechanisms for this discovery.

Context binding addresses the challenge that early authentication signaling may use a different transport protocol than the final link-layer connection. When the mobile device arrives at the candidate authenticator, it must securely bind the link-layer-independent context (peer and authenticator identities, keying material) to the link-layer-specific context (link-layer addresses). The binding can occur before or after the peer changes attachment points, and it requires a secure mechanism such as short-term credentials established during early authentication.
sections.eli5: Two challenges: first, finding the target network to authenticate with before you move there. Second, making sure the keys you got early still work when you actually connect with your real link-layer address.

sections.title: Security and Open Issues
sections.content:
Early authentication introduces new security considerations. A resource consumption denial-of-service attack is possible: an attacker can send unprotected early authentication messages to legitimate peers or candidate authenticators, forcing them to waste computational and bandwidth resources. Mitigation strategies include non-cryptographic packet filtering to accept early authentication messages only from known networks, and allowing only the peer to initiate early authentication, not the authenticator.

The channel binding problem is critical. Without proper channel binding, an authenticator can impersonate another authenticator or communicate false information, and this attack is easier with early authentication because the attacker does not need to be on the same link as the legitimate peer.

The RFC also identifies unresolved AAA protocol issues: defining whether a user can have multiple simultaneous early-authenticated sessions, managing session lifetime for early-authenticated states, distinguishing early authentication from normal authentication for billing, handling session resumption when a device cycles between networks, and supporting inter-AAA-realm handovers where the peer moves between different authentication authorities.
sections.eli5: An attacker could flood the network with fake early-auth messages. Also, a bad network could pretend to be the target network and intercept your keys. The system needs clear rules about when sessions expire and how to track who's authenticated.
